Every Caspr report opens the same way: an executive summary first, then the analysis, then the sources behind it. Knowing that shape before you start reading turns a long report into something you navigate in seconds, not something you scroll through blind.

Start with the **exec summary**. It states the conclusion before the argument — the way a report for a board should. Read it first even if you plan to read everything; it tells you where the sections that follow are going.

From there, the report moves through structured sections — market context, the core analysis, data exhibits — each building on the last. Briefs run flat, one section after another. Studies and Intelligence reports nest: sections carry sub-sections, and the depth of the nesting reflects the depth of the analysis.

You don't have to scroll to find your place. Open **Contents** — one of the switcher tabs beside the report (Contents · Ask Caspr · Edit · Outputs · Updates) — and you get a table of contents that scroll-syncs with what you're reading: the current section and sub-section highlight as you move, and tapping any row jumps you straight there. It's the fastest way to move through a long report without losing your place.

Every insight in the report carries an inline red dot — a citation you can click to see the source behind that specific claim. No hunting for a footnote or a separate sources page; the dot sits right next to the number it's proving. The full source list, if you want everything at once, is the report's final card.

Open the report, read the exec summary, use Contents to move around, click the dots when you want proof. That's the whole system.

Open your report.

A Caspr report is built like one a senior analyst would hand to a client, not a pile of generated text. Every section earns its place, and every number in it traces to a source.

It opens with the **executive summary** — the conclusion, stated plainly, before the supporting argument. If a reader has five minutes, this is what they take away.

From there the report moves into **market context** — the landscape your question sits inside: size, structure, the forces shaping it. This is the ground the rest of the analysis stands on.

Next come the **core analysis sections** — the actual work: competitive dynamics, scenario modelling, strategic implications, whatever your prompt and layout called for. This is where the report earns the word "analysis" rather than "summary." Depth scales with tier: a Brief covers this in 3–5 pages; a Study or Intelligence report goes several layers deeper, with nested sub-sections you can navigate from the Contents tab.

Findings are backed by **data exhibits** — charts, tables, and infographics tied directly to the data behind them, not decorative graphics. Each one carries the same citation discipline as the prose around it.

Every insight throughout the report carries an inline red dot you can click to see its source. And at the very end sits the **full source list** — every document, database, and feed the analysis drew on, in one place. No numbered footnotes scattered through the pages, no separate sources tab to dig for.

Conclusion, context, analysis, evidence, sources. The same structure whether the report runs three pages or a hundred — the ~100-page shape described here is what you get at Study depth.

See a full report.

Every insight in a Caspr report carries an inline red dot next to it. That dot is the citation.

Click it, and Caspr answers — through Ask Caspr — with the specific source behind that specific claim. Not a generic reference list, not a footnote number to cross-check against a bibliography: the source for that number, at the point where the number appears.

Do this for any figure in the report, as many times as you want. Trace a market-size estimate to the database it came from. Trace a growth rate to the report it's cited to. If you're about to put a number in front of a board, this is how you confirm it will hold up to the first question asked.

Want everything the report drew on at once, rather than one claim at a time? The full source list sits on the report's **final card** — every document, database, and feed used, in one place.

This is what separates a defensible report from a plausible-sounding one: you can check the work, not just trust it.

Trace an insight.

Yes — and you don't have to take that on faith, because every number is traceable.

Caspr's numbers come from the **weighing**, a methodology built to reason through data and structure conclusions, not simply generate plausible-sounding text. Behind it sit 25M+ **curated, credible sources** — documents, government databases, news feeds — not scraped web noise. The **sourcing** keeps that data current, so a market-size figure reflects this week's reality, not a training set frozen months ago.

The proof is in the report itself. Every insight carries an inline red dot; click it and Caspr shows the specific source behind that specific claim, right where the claim sits. Nothing in a Caspr report is unsourced — there's nothing left to invent, because every figure is grounded in a citation before it ever reaches the page.

That matters most in the moment you're not thinking about the tool at all — when someone in the room asks where a number came from. You answer with the source, not with "the AI said so."

Zero hallucinations isn't a slogan here. It's what happens when an analysis is built to cite, not to guess.

Verify it yourself.

**PDF** is the finished article — a boardroom-ready report exactly as Caspr produced it, laid out, formatted, ready to send or present as-is. It's included with every analysis, in your language, at no extra cost.

**Editable PPTX** is the same report, restructured into slides you can open in PowerPoint and change — reorder, rewrite, drop into your own template. It unlocks at the **Business milestone**, because editing is a Business-tier feature, not a formatting toggle.

Use the PDF when the report is the deliverable — a standalone document to send to a client or file for the record. Use the PPTX when the report is a starting point — material you need to reshape into your own deck before a meeting.

Both carry every citation. Adapting the PPTX doesn't cost you the sourcing that makes the report defensible in the first place.

Export your report.

Intelligence is Caspr's deepest analysis depth — built for decisions where being wrong is expensive. Where a Brief answers a single question and a Study builds the full picture, Intelligence goes further on both axes: broader sourcing across the 25M+ document, database, and news-feed library, and more reasoning passes from the assessment stage to stress-test the conclusion before it reaches the page.

The output format doesn't change — still a boardroom-ready PDF or editable PPTX, still every insight cited to a credible source. What changes is the rigor behind it, and the time it takes: Intelligence runs the longest of the three depths — up to 24 hours — because it's checking more angles and weighing more evidence, building a report designed to survive scrutiny in a board meeting or an investment committee, not just to inform one.

Pricing reflects the depth. Intelligence runs $300 within a Business or Enterprise Research Budget, or $399 à la carte with no subscription required — useful for a single high-stakes report without committing to a budget. Business is also where Intelligence unlocks in-budget, alongside data upload and editing.

Reach for Intelligence when the decision on the other side of the report matters: due diligence ahead of a term sheet, a market-entry call going to the board, a competitive assessment backing an acquisition. Corporate development teams use it to screen targets; investors, to back a diligence memo the partners will pick apart. For everyday questions, a Study at $80 or a Brief at $15 covers it for less.

Run an Intelligence report.

Start with the report you already have, not a blank deck.

At the **Business milestone**, every report includes an **editable PPTX** — the same analysis, restructured into slides rather than pages. Open it in PowerPoint and it behaves like any deck you've built by hand: reorder slides, rewrite headlines, drop in your firm's template and branding.

From there, adapt rather than rebuild. Keep the sections that carry the argument — the exec summary, the core findings, the exhibits that prove them — and cut what your specific audience doesn't need. This is where **Edit mode** earns its keep beforehand too: if a section needs to read differently for this board, revise it in the report first, then export.

The one thing not to do is strip the citations on the way in. Every insight in the PPTX still carries the sourcing it had in the report — keep it. A board deck that can answer "where did this number come from" is a stronger deck than one that can't, and stripping citations to make slides look cleaner throws away Caspr's entire advantage.

Fifteen minutes and an editable deck gets you further than a blank template and a week.

Build your board deck.

It depends on the analysis depth.

A **Brief** delivers **PDF** and **Markdown**. A **Study** or **Intelligence** report delivers **PDF, PPTX, XLSX, CSV, and Markdown** — the full set, not a subset you have to unlock.

That base set is included in the analysis price, generated natively in your own language — not English, translated after the fact. You choose formats and language at the **gate**, before the report runs.

Want something beyond the base — an extra format, a second language? Each one is generated and priced as its own output: PDF, DOCX, XLSX, and CSV run **$5**; PPTX runs **$10**; Markdown is always free. Add them at the gate or later from the **Outputs** tab — either way, the price sums into the button before you commit. [VERIFY exact figures vs .agents/pricing-model.md §4.6]

Generate your report.

Yes. English isn't assumed and it isn't a default you're stuck with — Caspr is multilingual by default, and your working language is included in the base price, generated natively in that language rather than translated after the fact.

Each **additional** language is its own output — a full rewrite of the report, not a format swap — generated in whatever formats you choose and priced per output, the same table used for extra formats. [VERIFY per-language pricing vs .agents/pricing-model.md §4.6]

Pick your languages at the **gate**, before the report runs, or add more later from the **Outputs** tab without touching the underlying analysis. Either way, the report you already have stays exactly as it is — you're only choosing what gets rendered from it, and in which language.

Add a language.

At launch, Caspr runs on a single template — one style, applied consistently across every report.

Style is doing more work than it sounds like. It governs density, vocabulary, how charts are treated, overall length, and whether appendices appear — the texture of the report, not just its skin. You set it before generating, at the **gate**, and choosing it there costs nothing.

Changing style **after** generation is a different action. "Make it denser," "add an appendix," "more visual" — each of these is a re-generation, not a preference toggle, and it's metered as an output like any other post-generation change.

Custom, user-built templates aren't part of the launch scope — one Caspr-designed template, well executed, beats a menu of half-finished ones.

Set your style.

Ask Caspr is the conversation that lives with your report — a scoped analyst you can question about the work in front of you, not a general chatbot. Open the Ask tab and you will find two things: a read-only history of everything Caspr already asked and confirmed while scoping your brief, sitting above a live question box. Type a question about a number, a claim, or a section you want explained differently, and Caspr answers from your report and its underlying sources — nothing outside that scope, nothing speculative, and nothing pulled from a different analysis you have run. Ask why a competitor was ranked ahead of another, where a growth figure came from, or what the layout deliberately left out, and you get an answer grounded in the same sources the report itself was built on. Ask Caspr is live from the moment generation starts, not just after delivery. Watching the Theater build your report and want to know why a section is structured a certain way, ask. Waiting through a 15-minute run and want to sharpen your Research profile for future analyses, Caspr's get-to-know questions surface here too. One rule matters more than the rest: asking never changes the report. The Ask tab is for reading and questioning, not writing. If a question surfaces something you actually want changed — a section rewritten, a chart swapped, a claim restated — that happens in Edit mode, and it produces a new version. Ask Caspr is where you interrogate the analysis. Edit is where you act on it. Treat it as a standing line to the analyst who wrote the report, open for as long as the report exists — no extra charge, no time limit.

Every insight in your report carries an inline red dot. Click it, and Caspr answers with the source behind that specific claim — scoped through Ask Caspr, without leaving the page. No footnote to hunt for, no separate Sources tab to open, no page number to cross-reference. The number stays on screen; the source arrives right next to it, in context, the moment you ask. This is what makes a Caspr report defensible in a room where someone will ask where a figure came from. You are not trusting the claim on faith — you are tracing it, one click at a time, to a named, credible source, and you can keep asking follow-up questions about that same source if you need more than the citation alone gives you. The full reference list for the entire report lives on its own card at the very end — a complete bibliography, in case you want to review every source at once rather than one insight at a time, or hand it to someone doing their own diligence. Day to day, though, you will rarely need it: the red dot does the work of a footnote without the friction of one. This mechanic runs on the same engine as the rest of Ask Caspr — the same scoped, report-specific answers, just triggered by a click instead of typed by you. It applies to every insight in every section, from the executive summary through the data exhibits and appendices. If a number appears in your report, it carries a red dot, and that red dot has an answer waiting behind it. That is the standard analyst-grade output has to clear: not just a confident claim, but a claim you can defend, live, to whoever in the room asks first.

Versions is your report's timeline — reached from the report's **⋯ menu**, not the pane switcher (that row is Contents · Ask Caspr · Edit · Outputs · Updates). Every edit you save creates a new version, and Versions shows them in order — v1, v2, v3 — as rows you can open individually to read that state of the report in full. Beneath each version sit its outputs: the actual generated files, PDF, PPTX, and the rest, produced from that specific version. Outputs are pinned to the version they came from. Generate a PDF off v2, then edit again to reach v3, and that PDF still belongs to v2 — it does not silently update to reflect your latest changes. If you want a current file, you generate a new output from whichever version you are now on. This matters because it means nothing is ever quietly overwritten. An earlier version and the outputs generated from it stay exactly as they were, so you can compare what changed between two versions, revert to an earlier read of the analysis if a later edit went the wrong way, or hand a colleague the exact file you reviewed together last week without worrying it has since moved. Outputs are generated on command, not automatically on every edit — so editing a report does not quietly spend budget regenerating every file behind it in the background. You choose when a version is worth turning into a deliverable, and which format that deliverable should take. It also gives you an honest audit trail: if a stakeholder asks what changed between the draft you shared on Monday and the one you presented on Friday, the timeline answers that question without you having to remember.

Contents is your report's table of contents, and it moves with you as you read. As you scroll through the report, the current section and sub-section highlight in Contents automatically — you always know exactly where you are inside a hundred pages, even without looking at a page number. Tap any row and the report jumps straight to it, no scrolling required to get there. It works the other way too: keep reading normally and Contents keeps updating to track you. That two-way sync is what makes a long report navigable rather than a wall of text you have to scroll through blind, section by section, to find the one page you actually need. A Brief's Contents is flat — a short, single-level list, matching its tighter three-to-five-page scope. Study and Intelligence reports nest: sections expand into sub-sections in the list itself, mirroring the deeper structure those tiers deliver across a hundred pages. Use Contents to orient yourself the moment a report lands, to jump straight to the section a colleague asked about before a call, or simply to check how much ground the analysis actually covers before you commit to reading it end to end. It functions the way a bookmark pane does in a well-built PDF, except it already knows where you are without you telling it — useful when you are moving between the executive summary and a data exhibit thirty pages apart while prepping talking points for a meeting.

Updates is coming soon — not yet available. Once live, it will flag when new data could change a finding in a report you have already run, so a standing analysis can be refreshed with what has changed rather than rebuilt from scratch. Watch this space; for now, re-run a fresh analysis if the market has moved since your last report.

Theater is the immersive view you get while Caspr works — a live look at your analysis being built, section by section, rather than a spinner and a wait with nothing to show for it. Stay on it and you watch the report take shape in real time, the same structure you confirmed at the gate filling in with research as it happens.

The build moves through four stages, visible right there in Theater — **Learning → Analyzing → Generating → Creating** — so you always know roughly where the report is, not just that it's "working." Once it reaches **Creating**, Theater tells you directly: "Finalizing your outputs — new requests will apply to the next version." Nothing you ask for at that point is lost; it just lands in the next version instead of this one.

Open the side drawer and Ask Caspr sits alongside it: ask a question about what is being researched right now, or answer the short get-to-know prompts Caspr uses to sharpen your Research profile for future reports — a rotating family of message formats, up to three per run — all without losing sight of the build behind it. Collapse the drawer and you are back to the full Theater view, no progress lost either way.

Nothing you do here — watching, asking, answering — touches the report itself. Generation is atomic once it starts: no pause, no stop, no mid-run edit, by design. Theater is where you spend the wait, not where you steer the outcome. If something needs to change once you see it, that happens after delivery, in Edit mode.

Most reports finish inside 15 minutes, so Theater is built for a wait that short — something to watch, not a dashboard you need to babysit for an hour. It is also where the sourcing stage's live sourcing becomes visible: instead of a blank progress bar, you see the categories of research the analysis is actually pulling from as it works.

Caspr renders its findings as charts, tables, and infographics inside the report — a number rarely stands alone when a visual makes the finding clearer to a reader skimming for the headline. Every one of them is tied to its cited data, so a chart is not decoration sitting next to a claim; it is the claim, rendered, with the same sourcing standard as the surrounding text. Want something different once you see it? Open Edit mode on any visual and you can swap a chart type, adjust a table, or ask Caspr for a different treatment entirely — a bar chart instead of a line, a ranked table instead of a paragraph, a simplified view for a slide instead of a dense one for a page. Saving that change produces a new version, alongside any text edits you have made elsewhere in the report, and the prior version of the visual stays on the Versions timeline if you want it back. Charts and standard infographics render deterministically, so revising them is fast and does not touch the underlying data. A limited number of bespoke visual generations are included with each analysis, scaled to its tier, which covers the shaping most reports actually need before you run out. Every visual carries the same red-dot citation as the text around it, so a chart is exactly as traceable as the sentence describing it — nothing in the report gets to make a claim the rest of it does not have to answer for.
